blocks.x: I think that microphone will pick up everything in the room here so you don't have to talk any louder than just usual. You might start with that, but I think you can give your name first so that we'll have this identified when we go to listen to the tape.
Yeah, well, when are you ready?
Yes, we're ready right now. It's all right.
My name is Luis Teo.
Were you older or younger than your brother Lorenzo Jr.?
I'm after him. I'm second after him.
So a little young, but you don't mind when were you born? He was the oldest one of them. He was the oldest?
He was the oldest of all of them.
How many were in your family?
Well, we were five altogether. Two brothers and three sisters.
Mrs. Long is one of your sisters.
That's my sister. That's the youngest one of all.
There's another sister that married, I know, one of the Boccage brothers.
Mrs. Song saxophonist. They were from Mexico.
They came from Mexico? I've heard that, I didn't know if it was true.
From Tampico, Mexico.
Really was true.
And my grandfather's sister was a guitarist. And they moved here after my grandfather died. My grandmother moved here, which I had an uncle, Marcus Teo. He was an also crying at us.
Never knew of him at all.
Well I knew. And he was the oldest of the family. And I came, I had an aunt after him. She was also a guitarist. But they never was made famous, in better words. After they left Mexico, excuse me.
Did you hear anything, I was going to ask you to interrupt, anything you know about the family in Mexico, where they studied music or which city they came from?
That's just before my time.
You never heard them say whether they came from Mexico City or down that far or where it was?

Tampico, Mexico. I know where they came from. Tampico, Mexico. Tampico. Tampico and somewhere around in Veracruz. You were in two places. But for, when you're a youngster, you don't remember these things. Yes, that's right. Well, they came here. They had my uncle Marcus. He was a crying at us. Well, and my uncle Louis, he was also a crying at us. He was a bastoon and an old boy at playoff. Now, he was older than your father, was he? He was older than my father. But Marcus was the oldest of all of them.
Do you know when, do you have the dates when they died and were born by any chance? Or do you, could you guess about when it was?
I wouldn't be able to give you that right off the reel.
Yes, I know it's difficult.

And because I was pretty young and I don't remember these things, but I probably might be able to get it for you. When you were born and all that kind of stuff. Then I had my father. He was also a kind of saxophone, a bastoon player.
That was Lorenzo Senior.
Lorenzo Senior. That's my father. Well, he was, then my brother followed in his footsteps. That came, he played all the reed instruments.
Yes. How much older was he than you? Do you remember about?
Well, I'm 65 now. He would be about, about, about 68 years of age, 69 years of age.
Yes.
And, we all learned music, previous times, just from childhood. As we came along, we learned music.
You mentioned you studied solfegge.

Solfegge, catechism music and solfegge. We didn't have, in them days we had to learn the notes from the catechism. And then we had to hear a tone of an instrument. And we had to sing solfegge from note to note. And, that was to improve the hearing of the, of the young figure. Lots of times, you know that to be a fact, that the musician, if today you take a band of music and they have a band, they are, they doesn't have the, the proper hearing. You'll be right, that fellow will be wrong. Now, if you doesn't have a keen hearing for that particular part of the music, well, you'll never detect that. But in music, you got to have a wonderful hearing. Aside from that, you're not right. Because you can't tune right. Hear my rhetoric. Let's go right. Right. And, these days, them days we had to learn. But I was a fellow this way. I played and they forced me to play.
But how old were you when you started on the solfegge?
I think I was a boy about, somewhere around five or six years old. That to know what I was doing.
I know some people have told me that your father and your uncle, especially, would make people study the solfegge for three or four years, maybe before they could take up an instrument.

That's right. Provided with hearing. Hearing. You see, they were great teachers. That's one thing they were. They were great teachers. They turned out many, many, many scholars. They turned out, such as George A. Paquet. He was a famous guy. He was taught by my uncle. And, um, there's, uh, Asheel Batty. They were all taught by my uncle. In better words, my uncle played with Sousa's band. He was clarinating in Sousa's band. Uh-huh. And, uh, later he got in the world, because he just become the big writing and transporting music. They made, he made pretty nice pieces of money on transporting music. In them days they had, you'd buy a copy of music, and there was no orchestration behind it.
Yeah. He'd arrange all of them.
So I had to get someone to arrange this orchestration. And that's where my uncle and my father did well.

Well, uh, before I forget it, um, some people, um, Ricard Alexis was one that told us that, I believe your uncle, Louis Thiel, was over in Bay St. Louis for a while. Do you remember? Yes, we lived there a while.
Mm-hmm.
The whole family? Your father too?

Yeah, my father too. We lived there a while. Well, I attended school, Portland, B. St. Louis, and my father had a band that was called the Prumwood Band. And, uh, that's when my brother played his first parade.
Really? Oh, really?
He played his first parade at Nine Years a Beach.
Mm-hmm.

And, uh, during the First World War, he was, uh, my brother left from here and went to Chicago. And, uh, during the draft, they wanted him, uh, went on the rehearsal with the Bay, Illinois, and they, uh, wanted him as a bandwriters. Because he knew this transposition business to and fro. He could take a B flat tire and make a monkey with that.
Make any of that.

And, uh, that you wanted, he didn't have to use from the A, C, E, or B flat. All he wanted was that B flat. And he could pull it out to make any tone that you want out of it. Because he was a fellow, he didn't believe in carrying a whole lot of instrument with him. Do you know that?
Yeah, he'd take that B flat clarinet and play any part or any key, you know, like, it was just a key or something.

I remember once Bunk Johnson told me that he came to the, he didn't, wasn't a regular member of the Eagle Band, but one day he went there to play with the Eagle Band, and they said, what's the matter, you only have your one clarinet. He said, I think I can do it all right. That's right. And he didn't need all those others.

So he didn't need all of them, you see. So, uh, that made him kind of a thing, because Dully wanted him to be a bandwriters in the Eagle, Illinois, but then he, he didn't care about that because he wasn't married and his wife was about to have a child. And he even figured I was going in the army, so he decided he'd come back here again. And also he'd written a lot of numbers.

Oh, yes. I know Barney Bigard told me that he sold a lot of numbers to Ellington, or quite a few, anyway. Do you remember which numbers those were? Did he ever tell you which ones he sold? Later, Duke put his name on them, and then Barney put his name on, I think, Mood Indigo or something.

Mood Indigo was right. Well, that's what he made, he sold, a sophisticated lady was originally written by Lorenzo Keough, and that was written right here on Havana Street at 2404. That was before he went to New York. Then he had Mood Indigo and Mood Glow, and him and Steve Lewis, which I would like that they made a number of, uh, Lorenzo Teo and Steve Lewis, Harlem Hot Shot. You tell me it was a pretty hot number. That was the title of it? That was the title of it. Harlem Hot Shot. I never heard, I never know anything about it, but I heard some people say that it was played over the A.
Yeah. They might have changed the name of it too, you know, give it a different title.
They do that. Well, then there was, uh, Sidney Bishy. Oh yes. Sidney Bishy was also got a lot of ideas from my uncle and my father. Then he came up with my brother.
He came up with my brother. That's my sister. How are you doing?

How are you doing? My brother, my mom. How are you doing? I'm Colin. How are you doing? How are you doing? How are you doing? Do you remember me at home? How are you doing? Dejan. Dejan. Dejan. Oh yes. Oh yes. Indeed.
Oh, excuse me.
Excuse me.
Sorry for glad to meet you. How are you doing? All right. See, we were talking about some of the different numbers that your brother wrote. Yeah. Well, there was...
How about the Red Man Blues? Did he write that? Red Man Blues? I don't know. I don't know.
Bruce Cochard have a record of it if you ever want to hear him. He played a clarinet and a Red Man.

Yeah. I wouldn't know. I know that he played many a number such as, uh, um, I know he had clarinet solo one time in, uh, I wish, at P. Rowe's number. Um, Sister Kate. I wish I knew what it was. Sister Kate. Well, he, uh, he did a lot of numbers, but I don't know what they were because he was in New York and I was here. Of course, he didn't believe in going around a whole lot of publicity. He knew that, uh, New York had a lot of racket to it. And, uh, he knew that if in case he would get, uh, they'd tell you, well, uh, give me your copy now and I'll, I'll look it over and probably, uh, I'll, I'll tell you what it's all about in about two, three weeks or so. Well, of course, they got a chance of taking all your number down, you see. And with a few different arrangements, a few bars that they're different, well, they got your number. You can't get back at them because they, they have your under, they got you.
Yeah, a few little changes and they can still copy right now.

See? Yeah. Well, your original copy when you go to cope with that, this is your copy. This is his copy. Well, they didn't change the bar. You, you, you can't, you can't fight them for that. Well, he made a lot of numbers that I don't know anything about. Yes. But he's got a daughter that's in New York. They, he did pretty well because I know he bought a home in, um, in New York, in Mount Juan in New York.
He stayed up there when he went up to Pierron, did he, and stayed on?

Yeah, he left Pierron. He left, left here and went on up there, he said. And he was going out for yourself. He told Pierron that up in case jazz was getting, be popular down here and they were unable to, they want youngsters that can produce. He said, I can produce. I can play. I want you to get some other fella that can play that hold me up. Well, no, you wanted that particular part of, uh, this way of his band, the way that he wanted it. Well, he said, if y'all want it that way, I'm going to New York. And he left. And Pierron often times told me that I'm sorry that I never did listen to Big Brother, he used to call him. Yeah. He said, he often told me, he said, if I, I should change my, my band. And so, he didn't, so my brother went to New York, he made, he made famous circles.
He had made one trip up there, I think they made records up there though with the band.
Oh yeah, uh-huh. They had, they made several trips. He made a trip with, uh, with, uh, Ninel Perez, and, uh, to Chicago. He would have wished to about introduce jazz in, uh, in Chicago.
That's what I'd heard back, well, you remember the year about when that was?
Just a minute, if I can, excuse me.
Sure.
This is some of the old-timers.
Oh yeah, that's the, uh, Esquire, yes. I have a copy of that.
Yeah, Esquire. Well, you know, you know all that. Yes. Well, you see a picture of them that, when they're introduced to the, uh, uh, in Chicago.
Oh, that's right, that's that band, the, uh.
Yeah, that was Manuel Perez, and, uh, Louis Cottrell. Yeah, or Sonia Caffey. That was my brother, Lorenzo. Yes. And this was the latest of Armand Pirou's band.
Oh yes, uh, Peter Boccage has a picture just like this, too, I think.
Yeah, that was, uh, that was Pete here. Uh-huh.
Yeah, there we go.

This is a little British subject. It was named Clarence Segari, who was a bass tuba. And that's Steve Lewis, Charles Bookreis, Juanique, Juanique, that's my brother. And this is Luca Trev. Now, that was the whole outset here that went to New York and played at the Roseland.
At the Roseland Ballroom there?
That's right.
I forgot where they were. I noticed this is addressed, this autographed by...
Armand Perron, he gave me, that was to me. To? Louis Teo.
Louis Teo. And it was February 28th, 1924.
That's about the time they went to New York, was it, or a little later?
No, that was just after they come back from New York, I think it was. And this is some of the old timers. You asked me the name of some of the old timers.
Oh, yes. You think this date is about right? They give it 1915 here. 1915, that's about right. I think that's about right.
Mm, that's about right. Yeah, there was a lot of them that I knew in here. There was a... There's a fellow that... I don't know if you all have known him.
Johnny St. Cyr. Yes, I know him very well.
And I know that there was the old line with Ben. Oh, yes.
This is Jimmy Noon, is it? Yes, Jimmy Noon.
This is Jimmy Noon.
I have a better picture. I was out and saw Johnny St. Cyr about two years ago. Stayed at his house for over a month.
That's all the tuxedo.

We went out with Professor Mineta, and he gave me his copy. He didn't give it to me. He loaned it to me, and we made a new copy of that. It has Clarence Williams sitting down here on the floor, which you can't see on this one. They cut off Terence Williams on this picture, but the rest of the band is all...
I know the old Octave Gasper and Vic Gasper, Tatone and...
I never got to meet the Gasper.
Jackson, Vic Gasper.
This is your brother here, the tall... That's right. He was rather tall, about your height, would you say? Just about my height.
Yeah, he was about six foot, six foot two, six foot three, like that. That was Kimball, and it was... Manuel Perez.
Manuel Perez. Manuel Perez. Manuel Perez. Manuel Perez. Manuel Perez.

Kimball. Juanjo Tatone. Alexander. This boy, I forgot his name. That was from Algea. Drummer. Drummer. Jackson, I believe his name. They give it here as Baby Matthews. Baby Matthews. That's Bill Matthews.
One of the three or four of them that played. Yeah.
A lot of them I forgot their name. That's a good picture there.
I was wondering if they really did go to Chicago very early then. Do you remember, you say you went with Manuel, did the whole band leave at one time to go up?
Yeah, that's five that left there. They left there to go up. They all left together. To go to Chicago. So, 1915.
That was about that.
1915, 1914, 1915, somewhere around the world.

I've met quite a few of his pupils, your brother's pupils up there. People like Darnell Howard studied with him. Yeah. Older Simeon, who was born here, he died last year. Older Simeon, but he was one of the better clarinetists up there. He studied with your brother too.
He turned out a pretty fine little scholar too. And then I tell you, he had a scholar, he had a fellow by the name of Tony Gardina. Oh yes. Gardina.
He was the pupil of your brother's.

That's right. He was a, he had a barbershop here on Liberty in Byron. He, he, he taken lessons from my brother and he was made famous. He went to Chicago and he stayed in Chicago. And also there's Eddie Sherry, he played with the Chicago police band. Remember him? Yeah, he's the one.
Yeah.
Eddie Sherry, he played with the police band. And he was also a scholar, my brother. Barney Begard was a scholar, my brother. Yes, Barney talks about it.
Yeah.

And Simeon too. Simeon and little Elliot Taylor. Oh, he was a good. Yeah. Little Luke of Trell. All of them was his scholars. He had many of them that he turned out, he turned out a lot of white scholars too, but I don't know them so very well. Yeah. And they had Humphrey, Humphrey was a pretty good student also part of my uncle. Which one?
Which, which is the, the young Willie? Willie Humphrey. The young Willie Humphrey. Yeah, yeah, young Willie Humphrey.

He, he come up in part of the town. He got a lot of information from my uncle. And they, the jazz music of them days, And they, started off with jazz. They were a lot of musicians that didn't know how to read music. And those that didn't know how to read, those that didn't know how to read music. Of course. The guy that didn't know how to read music. You used to hear him. And by that. He went in and he played what he heard. We gonna play this number. He'd know that. He'd know that. Yeah. stuff gonna fake it in with some variation and that filled it in. Do you understand my point? And that's what made jazz. Well that sounded good to the public's ears and what made it popular. Everybody liked it and that began going on and going on. That's with Dixieland jazz band. But for my part at all, I love Dixieland jazz band, but I love opera. Can't take that away from the instrument that counts. The blending of the tones. Rock and roll, I'm out. That's out. Poets, when it comes to this progressive jazz, that's out. You can take anybody today, stick a saxophone in his mouth and let him hear something and just let him make a, just a few notes in there, just so it sounds, that it, it just hit the marks together with that. And if he can hear another note, it changes that, to change that sound from that sound and then he, he, oh, he's got it. Yeah, he thinks he's ready to play a job. He's got it. Do you understand my point? That's what I, that's hard to interpret. Of course, he might have a different eye, you might have a different eye. That's right. Dixieland is right. Huh? Dixieland is right. That's the truth. Because the guy, you look into it, the fellas that go to work and say, I'm a musician, I know. When they stick that piece of music before you gotta know what you're doing. You gotta read that stuff. Now him, he don't know nothing. Now I'm gonna, I'm gonna phrase something to you that, Bichet was one of the greatest of all of them. In that hearing proposition. Bichet never did learn music. Bichet had a wonderful hearing. Only after Bichet went away from me. Bichet then became, he met my brother in Chicago. He met other good clarineters. He met Cairns William and those fellas in New York. Well, he come up. They got in him. They told him, you, you, won't you do this, study this, do that. They, they, they broke him in. They got him there. All right, now you know, he, he got a number that's out there. It's, uh, it's a French, uh, pretty flower. That's a wonderful number. That's a pretty number.
Yes, it is.
Well, if you notice, there's another number that came out, right after that. And it's been playing on American bandstand quite often. And that ain't no more than the whole originator of 33.
Sort of a copy of that. That's right. I don't remember.
It took seven years before, um, this man got his number published. You see my question? That's right.
That's right.
How it was, how they changed it. After that they give it another name. He's dead. We can play it now.
Yeah.
What is he not going to do? He ain't doing nothing. It's a trick in all that stuff.
Well, I was going to ask Mr. T.O. if you remember your, uh, uncle, I understand was a conductor of a symphony orchestra for a while.
That's right. He was a conductor of a symphony orchestra. He had it de-organized one time.
Do you remember when that was? Is that in your day that you can remember anything about it or before when you were so young?
Well, yeah. I remember that because they tried to force me to get in it. Oh, really? And I was, I played hooky from that.
What were you supposed to play?

Clarinet. I was supposed to play the seat clarinet. And, cause my brother ain't be playing clarinet and I was supposed to take the seat clarinet. So play, play in there and I run out and play hooky. But I did go around that hall and listen to them play. That was at St. Catrins Hall.
Well, they played up there.

Yes. They had rehearsals there. Yeah. There was many of them that, uh, was there. It was such as, um, uh, all the Gasper boys. And, uh, two Gasper brothers and they had, uh, Professor MacDonald. He's a dentist. You remember him? Yeah. Yeah. He was a pianist. He was a pianist. And, uh, he was, uh, also there. And, uh, volto. That's the violin. Violin. And they had, uh, Nickerson also. He was violin. Then they had, uh, Camille Nickerson also, a fine pianist. That's Professor Dixon's daughter. Dixon.

She's in Washington now. I think that's the one. That's right. She went to the Conservatory of Music. I believe Mr. Bollier told me he was there. What's his first name, Harold? You know, the pianist? He played cello and other obols.

Oh, yeah. That's, uh, that was another very fine musician. There was, uh, Bollier. Uh, now, another, another little fine pianist that she's teaching now, uh, Mrs. Johnson. She teaches music in one of these public schools. She's a very, very, very fine pianist. Oyama Johnson. She lives out here on Havana Street. But she never played in no band. But she's a very, very fine musician. A person that knows that whatever she reads, she puts it down. She knows what she's doing.
Yes. You say your brother lived there, too, on Havana Street?
Yeah, he lived right back. He bought, that was his house back there. He sold it when he went to New York, when he married home in New York.
Do you remember the dates when your, the date when your brother died? About what year?
Year. It was on Christmas Eve, 1933. 1933. That's when he died, Christmas Eve. And he was buried on, and he sent, sent his brother from New York here.
Back here, buried.
And he was buried here. It was on Christmas, New Year's Eve. So, just to, there's some law that I'm thinking of New York that they had to keep a body of that certain time. I don't know.
Yeah.
So, if that's what you gentlemen want.
Yes. I was going to ask a few more questions. I'd like to bother you too much.
Yeah. Go ahead. No.
Did your father play in this symphony orchestra too? Or did he ever conduct any?

No. No. My father, he, he did not conduct any, that I know of. Probably when he was, he was, he traveled a great deal. He traveled partly all over the United States. He traveled with great shows such as Billy Cassandra.
Oh yes, I've heard people talk about that show.
Yeah. He traveled with, he traveled with, he's a fellow who played, my father was a man who played a solo of Minnie Ha Ha. That's a very, very complicated piece of music.
Remember?

Minnie Ha Ha. And I don't know what he meant to have that copy yet. And that was an arrangement that was all written by my father and my uncle. They didn't have, they just had a suit. They had, they just had a suit and copy of it. And that was written by them. They were married to Northern Ireland.
It seems to me more of the old time musicians, they all talk about your brother as, usually they refer to him as the most famous one of the clarinetists in the family.
That's right. He was. Not saying in prison or trying to any book here, that family, he was one of the greatest.

You don't have to because everybody else does. He could tell that if he was down here and getting the street behind him when they had five or six others supposed to be great out there. That's what he used to tell who was who.

That's right. I was wondering more about your father now. Quite a few people will tell us about your uncle Papa, they call him, didn't they? That's right. That he played in some of the dance bands and other bands that they talk about. But very few people tell us which bands your father worked with. Did he ever do much dance work? Or a brass band?

That's right. My father, my father from the time, they were one of the greatest bands of all of them. That was the time of Teo and Dublade. They had a band of the arms. That's been a long time. Then my father. Then my father, he was a, he was a, had a band, Promo's band.
Which band is it?
Promo's band. That was Bay St. Louis.
Oh yeah.
Then he traveled so much that he went with, he was with a show and a, Billy Cassand show.
and Richard and Pringle. That's probably why we don't hear so much about him.
He was traveling all over around St. Francisco and Mexico. He was all over, part of all over the United States.
How long did you live in Bay St. Louis? You mentioned you were, or your brother was only nine years old when he was over there. You were about six then.
Yeah, we lived over there partly about seven or eight years.

Seven or eight years, a long time. Do you remember Oguise, the basement over there? Oguise? Yeah, yeah. He died a few years ago. I used to go over there and tell him. You did? Sure. Yeah. They had a family band. They made a little later. Yes, you know. Yeah. His daughter, me, of Jana and so on. I would like to ask you, Mr. Dale, do you remember approximately when the family moved to New Orleans from Mexico? Of course, that would be several years before you were born. And I wondered if you knew just about what year that would be.

No, sir. I wouldn't be able to tell you that. Probably I could get it for you. But I wouldn't know. Yeah, when I knew that was long before I was born, that was before my father got married. My father got married here.
Oh, I see. How far before was that?

My uncle Marcus, he left from here. He never did come back here anymore. He didn't like it. Oh, I see. He left from here and he went back to Mexico. And he never heard from him anymore. I understood that he had a great big coffee plantation somewhere in Brazil. I don't know. Really? He might have another family somewhere out there. I don't know.

By the way, I was going to ask, I'm just writing down here on the box of tape so I could identify the box with your name. How do you spell your first name? Do you use the Spanish spelling or just the regular?
L-O-U-I-S.
And did your uncle the same spelling?
Lewis, yeah. Same spelling.
Because I thought it might possibly be there's a Spanish way. Is it L-U-I-S?
No. We always use L-O-U-I-S. Tio, well, you know, that's...
Did your folks speak French or Spanish? Was it more of a Spanish family or more French?

They didn't know a word of English. Only thing they knew was French and Spanish. They didn't know anything at all. They didn't know no word of English at all. Of course, they would ask you what you were talking about, but they didn't know. My aunts, they all died. They died pretty old. One of them just died. My family, I don't know. I don't know.
You were talking about your aunts and your family speaking French.

They all... One of them... One of them not died... Just died not so many years back. And I think it was near around 1949. And she lived to be at the age of 80 years old. And she couldn't talk the word of English. No. Not a word of English. Well, what she could tell you in English, well, it took somebody who really understood her, you know. Yeah. Because she used to mix it all up. She thought she was doing all right.
Yeah.

Well, I had one last night that died that was due to feeding to you. Never did speak English at all. All she ever just speak was French and Mexican. The language. She didn't know anything at all concerning the English language.
I suppose, naturally, you were brought up to speak English, French, and Spanish.

I was. I... Like I told you, I was kind of a little bad boy. I learned the French language pretty well because they didn't talk nothing else to us. French. And, uh, little Spanish. I know pretty much of that because I... Of course, I got out of practice because they used to speak amongst themselves. My father and my... And his sisters and my uncle, they used to talk amongst themselves. And oftentimes, especially, you used to keep a keen eye on what they were saying, you know. Yeah. And watch the lip. And you probably used to get something in the ad. And then after I grew up, I used to ask my father. Then my mother was well-wrist, but if she knew... While I married my father, she knew the language pretty well. So, uh, that's our guess that I picked up some of that language. But I certainly loved it. I certainly am sorry that it didn't live long enough so I could probably learn it. Yeah. French it all together.

I know some people have told me that your brother seemed to have a French accent. I mean, certain people have told me how he would talk. They would start quoting, you know, saying certain things. And they would try to imitate a French accent. Do you remember? Did he have sort of a French?

Yes, he did, because I'll tell you why, because, you see, he was taught in French, in better words, he spoke French and English language. He spoke the French language frequently and he's read it. Also written it. He knew that because he learned that. Like I told you, I was kind of a little bad boy. I didn't, if they tried to catch me to do that, I was gone. Yeah, I didn't want to get part of that. I didn't, all I wanted to do, I love horses and I used to like to be around horses and I like to be doing something. Sometimes I was an animal, but I loved them. When it came to be confined to one thing only, I couldn't do it. I couldn't do it, I couldn't see myself doing it. That's the reason why I tell you, I learned music, I learned clarinet, I learned the violin from AJP. I didn't finish learning, but anyhow, I started with him. Carinet, I learned that with my father and my uncle and my brother. My brother was the last that I had dealing with. Brother, he couldn't do too much with me because I could run away from him. I would tell him what I wanted, see. I was a bad boy. Well, I'm sorry to take what, but not only that, but probably I would help somebody else, not myself, because for my part, it's all over. I love music very much. In better words, I really love opera. Boys turn on the radio and hear all that jazz and stuff.

Well, I was going to ask this about your uncle. People have told me that he sometimes didn't really like jazz so much that he liked classical music more. I know one man who was a pupil of Manuel Perez, Natty Dominique, who's in Chicago now. He knew your brother very well, too. And he told me when he was a kid, his father liked opera and his brother still lives over here on Robertson or some street down near there. And he used to be a good singer. And he said sometime your father would hear, your uncle would hear a band in the street, you know, on a wagon. And he'd come running in their house. He didn't want to hear it. He thought that music was not good.

That's right. That's right. He didn't have that attitude. Yeah, he didn't approve of that. He didn't let go of that. Because he'd tell you that was outrageous. He didn't believe in that. He'd tell you that off the wheel. I don't see why did they allow that. He said, that's nothing to it. You know, in better words, we used to call them in the old Creole way, routiniers.
Oh, yes. I remember.

Routiniers. Routiniers. Routiniers. That's right. Routiniers. He used to say all the time, a bunch of routiniers. See? They don't know what they're doing. But they got along though, you know. But he didn't like that. He was a fella that was brought up with classic music. And I'm plenty behind it because I really love it. I don't know how you all feel about it, but I really love classic music.
I was trained with classical music. You were on violin. I play violin myself. But I like the jazz very much, of course, now.

Well, I'm going to tell you. Now, I don't condemn the jazz. I like the distance of Dixon and jazz. Why? Because I tell you that they got so much variation, so much clean variation that's understood in a piece of music. Because if a person got a keen hearing, you go to work and make a variation in some part, and then fall in right all the time, you're a professional. You know what you're doing. Because when you take an actor, he's got a script to read. And often the time he failed on that script. But he got to add something to that script. And they tell you that. That often time, an actor, he'll fail in his script, but it's fulfilled. And he'll fail. Why? Because there's something that comes to him and he fakes it in there.
Yeah.

You understand? He fakes it in there and it comes in there. Well, the only thing that a person has to do is to, if that fitted in there, cancel the other part that you had in there before. If that get in there right, let it be like that. You're not losing no money, is that right? That's right. See? Right? Yeah. And that's the same thing about music. As I said, you've got to have a keen hearing. And my uncle and one of them fathers had one of them things. Because he did just naturally. If my brother also, my brother would say, here's your music. You know your lesson? That's the kind of fellow he was. Do you know your lesson? Yeah. Well, alright, then let's get together and let's hear what you've got to say. Well, he was a friend of the shop. He'd tell you, well, go ahead and run over your instrument and start your lesson. I'm going off. Gone. Went back somewhere. But he had that with you.
Still hearing you. Every note you play.
Yeah. When he'd come back and say, ah, ah, ah, ah, give me that ball right there over and over again. You remember?
Well, I was telling him, a couple of times he gave me my dollar back and took a message to my dad. I didn't know my lesson. I'm not taking it. That's right.

That's right. He'd tell you you didn't want your money. Right. I remember right down the valley street, a fellow came to him and he said to him and he took several lessons with me. And he told the boy, he said, let me tell you something. I want to talk to your daddy. He did. He went and spoke to the boy's daddy. He said, listen, it's no use you wasting your money or trying to give me that money because I don't want it. Because I can't do nothing with your service. He just doesn't have the hearing. He didn't want it. He didn't want it. That's one thing he wouldn't take. But he knew what he was doing. All right. When he told you to sit down and sit down there and play that car and that he walked away from you. He knew what he was doing. And he'd come back and correct you. And that's the same way as my uncle. My uncle had that old sneaky way about himself. Papa. He had that sneaky way about himself. You know. And he'd come to him and he'd tell him. He'd tell him, you see. He said, you see son. What that really did. Now let's see. Let's see you make that. He was easy going. Let's see you make that right there. You make that right there. And he said, uh huh. He said, but you didn't make that before. How did you make that right there? How did you make that right there? Now I want that to be. I want you to put that in there. That's supposed to be in there. That's written there. And that was the truth. He didn't backpike. He just. When he said, son. You see this lesson right there? Well you want. I want this in person. But you can run over this in tomorrow. And when you get out of time. You can run over this in. But I want this in here. Put it in. You better bring it back there. Put it in.

I think you do it over again. That's right. I was going to ask a little bit about the lessons that your uncle, for instance. Did he teach right at his home? Did he have a certain music room in his home? Did he ever teach more than one at a time? That is, did he have a whole class? And what about his class?

Well, if he had two or five pupils, he was using by themselves. Now if he had two, three pupils that he had pretty good, that's one thing that I had. That's one thing that he could give me. See my father was a fellow this way. Lewis, he's come to his son. He said, listen, come get your clarinet and your brother and we play some duets together. You know what I'm saying? That's what he did. That's what he did. And you had to stay down there and play duets with him. And he'd be correcting you. Well, it used to help out. And that's the same thing my uncle and my dad would do. When they had two scholars that were really good. And he was about to get out of the way. He told them, you and you, we all come together. He said, let's try some duets. We couldn't do it.
Did he teach at his home? At home, at home. Do you remember what he charged your lessons and your uncle when he was teaching?
Well, in that day, things were pretty cheap too. Sometimes 75 cents or a dollar. That thing was pretty cheap.
Did most of the pupils come more than once a week or how often would they have lessons, do you know?

Well, it's a cause. Some of them come, that's a cause in the door. They had some of them that was working and they wasn't able to make it once a week. Some of them used to come twice a week. Yes. Like a fellow like Eddasharie, he was a Baba. He had to, used to come twice a week, sometimes, sometimes once a week. It's according to how his business was going.
Oh, by the way, before I forget, did your uncles and your brother have another trade besides their music? Did they, somebody told me one of them was a cigar maker at Breeders?
That's right. My uncle, Papa, was a cigar maker.
Your uncle was. Your uncle was. Yeah. Your father, did he do what? My father, yeah, he was a bricklayer.
He was a bricklayer. Yeah, he was a bricklayer. I trade.
Well, that's right. I believe, um, remember, um, Louis DeLille, they called him big guy, Louis Nelson. A lot of people probably not knew him very well. I think he studied with your father.
That's right. Maybe your uncle too, I forget what he told us.
My uncle, he gave him a few items, he took them out of that from my father.
That's right, I think he said your father was a bricklayer, but somebody told me that once, I forgot. Did your brother have another trade too, or did he stick mostly to music?

No, my brother was strictly to music, all his life, he never did anything but music. That's the reason why I made him so famous, he could, there was nothing to music to him, just like drinking a glass of water. Because he never done nothing else in his life but that.

Now there were a few things that probably Ralph would like to ask too, Ralph's trying to learn clarinet a little, about your brother, do you remember what kind of an instrument he had? Anything about his instrument, if it was how many keys, or if it was Albert or system, or what kind of a clarinet it was? What maker or anything at all?
No, it was an Ebony, black Ebony, but I didn't know the name, but I forgot about it.
Would it be something like a French name, something like Buffet or something like that?
There's one of them, yes, but there's another one besides that Buffet, there was a... Oh, I can't see right now.
There's a French Selmer, there's a lot of French makes that we don't even know about, I guess.
Well, the instrument in them days, like, they didn't have as many keys, that is, metal keys, as the instrument of today. A hundred percent of that was open keys, you know, few metal keys.
I wondered if, if you could remember if it had those ring keys, or holes, on both the top and...
No, on the bottom, but not the top.
Not the top.
Uh-huh. They had the ring, they had the holes in the top.
Just a very big hole.
And you had the rings on the bottom. With the trill keys.
The trill keys, did it have two or three?

Two. Two trill keys. Mostly it would just be two. That is the old instrument, and then they came with the three. And they had three trillings on the above, on the above part of the clarinet. They had also two, but then they later on got a three.

So I don't know. I wondered if you, if you knew, of course he would be playing, as you say, B flat all the time, but I wondered if you, if he ever played the E flat in the parades. Oh yeah. Yeah. He noticed that picture. I remember that, he got an E flat on that picture.

On that picture, yeah. Oh, I hope to tell you. On the little band, I mean, on the, I don't know, that's fine. Yeah, right here. I could just, I never knew. Did he play it? E flat, isn't he? Oh, up here, sure. Oh yeah, sure. We can see. I saw that, as soon as you all opened it. Yeah, I never noticed that. I've seen that big. E flat. Now he had a whole family of clarinet.
He had a B clarinet, he had a B flat clarinet, A and a C. And you know, E flat, and he had a D. Oh, a D.
D clarinet. D, I don't believe I ever saw a D.

It's a heavy toned instrument, like the A clarinet. Yes. And the C clarinet is probably supposed to be mostly a youngster that is trying. A very toned, very soft toned instrument, the C clarinet. Then you got the E flat clarinet with a high, very high pitch. Did you know that? Yes. The E flat has a very high pitch. Now the D clarinet, they have a very deep tone and it has also a little bell on the part of it. Like an outdoor. Like an outdoor. Yeah, that's a D clarinet. Yeah. Well he had one also. Yeah. My brother had a D clarinet. He had a little bar. He used to play bassoon, but mostly when he was playing at Felice Crencini, Felice Crencini found him with the bassoon. Yeah. Yeah. He had a pretty expensive piece of instrument. Yeah, that was a big, yeah. Unless you couldn't very well buy it, but you wanted. Well, Felice Crencini used to love to hear him play that and he used to, he fought it to you. You know who Felice Crencini was. Yeah, that's it. The nightclub down at the lake. Yeah. He managed to play.
I suppose they were Saturday night, wasn't it? Yeah. I wondered if you ever knew about what strength of reed Lorenzo would use. Would he use a medium or a hard, a soft reed?

Well, I think that his reed on his instrument was mostly a hard reed because when he'd buy a reed out of the stove, he'd eventually always stick it to his mouthpiece and try it out. And he'd loosen the clip and stick another old reed underneath it and probably eat it, sand it down to the end and then take that clip off and then cut that reed. That would give it a stiffer pitch.
In other words, he'd make them to suit himself a little. Suit yourself.
So, it's according to the tone that he liked. If he had the tone, the pitch that he wanted, he had it at that. If he didn't like it, well, he'd cut it some more.
I wonder if he...

In better words, he used to carry a scissor and a needle and a tread and his pocket just like a tailor. Now, that seemed foolish, but that isn't. You see, when he was coming up, we had to learn how to make pads. He doesn't like the day that you had to buy pads. You can buy pads. We had pads that you had to get your cotton. You had to get the cotton and then you had to go to work and get some kid gloves or something of that kind, some light kids. You just cut the...put the key on top of that. And then take the print of the key, take your scissors and cut it around. Get your piece of cotton. Put it in there. Get your needle and stitch it all around and make your arm. And then get yourself some rod. Get your little candle and put it on top there and then melt that rod in there and then take this pad and press this pad and... You know, you're making your own key. You're making your own pad and your own carinet. You didn't have that. Today you can go down there and buy and make the pad you want. You didn't have that. You had to make your own pad. Well, of course, you could send your carinet to World Lines or Grunwald and them did and they'd pad it for you all right. They'd send to the manufacturer and get the pad, but then it cost you money. They all know how to make your own pad. That's the reason why I tell you, you used to do like a tailor, carry your needle and tread. I remember a slip. It was in the St. Louis Cemetery right down Denville and Claiborne. There was a funeral and my brother was playing, Nero my God to be. He broke a string in one of his keys. And he took a rubber band quick out of his pocket and stuck a rubber band on that thing and he trilled it. And they had the people in there that thought that was the greatest thing in the world. One of the greatest that was played. They never heard Nero my God to be played like it was played then. Well, that wasn't but a broken key. That's wrong time. You understand? That was a misfortune, but then it sounded good.
When he got that particular note he had to thrill it to make it sound like that.

And the people thought it was great. Thought that he had it or something, you know. Hey, they congratulate on it. And he turned around and he said, I wonder what they tell him to congratulate me about it. One woman said, young man, she said, you really didn't play that in your room? I got to be. And then after that I realized, I said, what happened? He said, I don't know you. I said, I noticed you took your clarinet down. He said, yeah, I took it down. I broke a spring underneath the key. And I said, that's what the woman must have been hollering about. He said, well, I had to do something. He said, you know, to finish that number.

Well, I was going to ask about the position of the teeth on the mouthpiece. Most clarinetists that I know put their upper teeth, they put the lower lip on top of the lower teeth, even then they bite on them.
The upper.
But a few people used their lip over both teeth. Well, then I... Marty Bigard does that. I wonder if he learned that from your brother. Do you know how your brother did or your father and the...

No, my brother had a way of his upper teeth. He would bite onto the mouthpiece? Upper teeth. Well, he had pressure against his upper teeth. In other words, he played clarinet so long that his teeth had been ground down in the shape of a mouthpiece. Mm-hmm. But for his biting on the lower teeth, no he didn't. He never, never... He covered those.
Yeah.
He had... In better words, that's the reason why he could use his tongue so well. Mm-hmm. On the...
Did your father and uncle too, if you remember, did they bite onto the... No, they had...
Get their teeth onto the... No, they had... When they taught a scholar, they tried not to make him bite it. Because when you're biting an instrument, you're... You're fouling it.
I think what Bill means, he means that they teach him to rest their teeth on the... Yeah, I know what you mean.

Yeah. But oftentimes, uh... Sometime you can foul it that way, you understand? The best thing is to keep the lower teeth from it. Yeah, the lower teeth. I'm wondering about the upper teeth, though, too. And let the instrument rest in on your lips. Yes.

Because you've got a better pressure, you've got a better way of using your tongue. I was just wondering about the upper teeth, though. If they covered the upper teeth, too. Some people, I think they call that the French system, a double embouchure, putting the lip over the upper teeth, too. And the upper teeth, too. Some people do that. Do you know if they ever taught that? Or played that way?
I don't know.
But I know, uh...

I'll tell you what. Here's the position that he would use his clarinet. If he had his clarinet, well, uh... When he'd stick it in his mouth, he would always, mostly have the pressure up above on his upper teeth. Yeah. He would never have his pressure down on you. He always had his upper teeth. In better words, if he turned and looked at you like that, he turned... But the clarinet would never go down. He kept the pressure on his upper teeth, not on his lower teeth. But the lip, of course, would close in. Yeah, sure. I don't know how close his teeth was to the reed, but I know that he never would bite it. Like you said, biting it. Yeah, I don't know. That would be biting. That would be closing your teeth on it. Because I don't believe... A fellow biting a reed... He's then putting strain on yourself because... Yes. ...for the pressure... He's putting it, he's pumping from here. Where you could say... Do-do-do-do-do-do-do... With your teeth. With your tongue. Where if you had your teeth in your mouth, then you'd be... You'd have to do... Hoo! Yeah. You'd have to pump it from here. Yeah, that's right, yeah. You see? And that, you had to blow it from your lungs. Where if you had your teeth free, well you could toot it from your tongue.

Do you remember any special exercises that your brother did or anything? When he practiced, did he ever practiced much at home in late days? Or after he learned to play, did he just play on the job and that was about all? Well, I remember when...

One year before you went to Chicago, my uncle Papaya came to him and told him, he said, You're going amongst some great, great musicians. And he said, when you leave here, don't let nobody food. He said, I know you've been a jazz player all your life, so you can play jazz. But you're going to meet some men that really do know music. And he said, you might confront with that. And sure enough, that's what he did. He got on in the room by himself. He didn't ask nobody for nothing. He just came in there and locked himself in the room. And he got all the music that he knew of, such as all the orchestration that my daddy had, and he had a beautiful number of Sally. And for at least an hour, an hour, an hour and a half, he'd run the scale, dramatic scale, tune through, up and down, up and down. He'd get out and went and take a drink of water. Do even sisters, come back there again, sit down and probably look at the paper, get back up and try and do the same thing. But when he went to Illinois, that's why I tell you he had an opportunity of being a bandwriter in the 8 Illinois, in that position as a first lieutenant. He met the bandmaster of the 8 Illinois, and they offered him to play at a rehearsal one Sunday. And he did, he went to, well they were looking for him with a whole caster instrument. You understand? They were looking for him with a whole family of clarinets, A, B flat, B and C. Well he didn't, he went there with his B flat clarinet, his mouthpiece, in his cool pocket here. stuff

That's something to laugh at. That's the truth. And his clarinet, his belt, he had it in his coat pocket, and his two parts of his clarinet wrapped in those steps. Well, you know what kind of impression that must have made on that bandmaster? Yeah, it was funny. What kind of clarinet play out like that? Yeah! You understand? And he told me that there stuck a piece of music, one of the hardest things that he ever read in his life, played in his life. And he came out there and he played that thing with that B-flat clarinet. And when he did, my bandmaster came out there and after this number was over and shook his hand and asked him what conservatory that he attended. He told me I never been to conservatory in my life. Who taught you? My father and my uncle taught you. Man, you're one of the greatest of the years. How do you do it? Out of all these men, out of these clarinet plays I got here, they can't do it. How do you do it? Well, I learnt that that way. Well, I'll give you a position as first, I'll give you band rider and I'll give you first lieutenant in the A's Illinois. Okay, no, I'm going back home. My brother's going to Norman. Well, his wife was about to have a baby. He came back home. Well, instead of me being sent to Norman, I didn't. I had my mother and I had my sister here and I had another one, two more of them, one of them that's dead and one that's living down on Rydell Street. Well, they were young and my father was dead and I wasn't so put.
Well, I was put in class 3B. That would be about 1918, the first world. That's the first world war. How many children did your brother have? Are they still living?
Yeah, they're living in New Rochelle, New York. Up in New Rochelle. They rented their home out in Mount Vernon and then they moved to, that's the suburb like you know.
Yes, this is the next town. I used to live up that way myself.
Yeah, well you know what it's all about. And there she got this home and she's got a daughter and also that played the flute.
Oh really?
And she played in one of these symphons in New York. She's in school, she goes to college I think over there and she played in one of them symphony orchestras there.
Did any of your family play the flute that is your uncle or father?

No, she's about the only one that played the flute. Then she's also got a son. He's taking after the footstep of his grandfather. Excuse me. He's taking after the footstep of his grandfather. He's taking a clarinet. That's Rose's children. That's Rose's children. Did you ever play in any bands, Mr. Teal? Did you ever play in any bands? Oh, I couldn't go for that. I couldn't teach a body dancing and I couldn't dance. Ever had me. Ever had me sitting down there going for somebody else to have fun. I used to like the girls plenty you know. I used to love the dance and I used to love the girls too. I couldn't do them two things at one time. But that's the reason why I never did. I never did do it. I was a fool. And I didn't ask me. They begged me, they begged me, they begged me. When my brother and them left from here to go to New York, Clarence Segarra, this boy here, British subject, he, my brother told me, he says, why not you play bass too before us? I said, how much the instrument costs? He always said it costs about $250, forget it. They got Clarence Segarra to play bass too. You know what I did? So you never did play in any, in any kind? No, no, no. But you did learn the clarinet song. Oh yeah, I tell you what I did, dude. I used to go around and play with some boys like that, you know. Just crazy and all that, having a little good time, getting in, give a little hiccups on them, we'd get together. And then the other kind of guys would be all around, you know. I used to get a guitar and they'd knock on the guitar and I'd get on the pin, I'd knock on the pin a little bit. That's all I cared about, you know, just for good time. Most instruments that I would use, he was my brother. My brother had a set of instruments, he had two sets of instruments. He had an old set of instruments and a set of instruments that was made present in. This boy, this Italian boy, that I tell you that he taught, made him a present of a whole set of instruments. Now he didn't ask him for it. But when he found out that he, for the good that he had done, he had given that. He had paid my brother to love him too. My brother, so I can't accept that. He said, oh yeah, you're going to take that. I bought that for you. He said, you may brew iron today. He said, today I don't have to stand up and eat nobody's hair, you're the barber, you know. I don't have to stand up and eat nobody's hair. All the thing I can do is sit down and blow. That's what he did, you know. I don't know, you might be a great fellow now if he's not dead.
I think he's dead now, I'm not sure. Who's that? Giardino. What's the name? Giardino. Yeah.

We had a lot of times, you know, at home. Like sometime my brother would get in there and my sister and the one that's living now in Oral Street, she and my sister here were two young people. All of them had already died out. My sister did it also. She'd do a piano she learned, piano she learned with Camille Nickerson. And my sister that's living on Oral Street. We often times used to get out of home and I'd get out. My sister'd come home. My brother would get his car in there. She'd get on the piano. I'd get a guitar. Make a little trio right there. Call a little wives, play music right there in the house. You'd get tired of it, get tired, get out and go. But there was a house of music all the time. What type of music did you play at home still? Any particular type or? Well, there are a lot of types. Such as high society and things of that kind, you know, and all. Lots of nice numbers. Or there's jazz propositions and all that. We had a down pat and mostly popular music we always did play. Some that was already written, you know, we knew it too. We learned. We played them. But I, for heaven, we always had music at home. We had a piano, we had, I had a guitar.
I was going to ask about your home again. Which part of town you were born in the New Orleans or not over in Bay St. Louis?
No, I'm born in the New Orleans. Right here. There was one that was born in Bay St. Louis and this is my youngest sister. Yes.

And your brother then, he was born right here in town. You know what part of town you lived in? Just about which street it would be that you were born on? I was born on Caleret Street. That's right out of- Oh, near St. Bernard Circle, down in that way?

No, right straight up over this way, Caleret. The street this side of this one is. The street that the Louisiana and the ticket though, that's Caleret and Clay. Caleret and Clay. Yes sir. I was born on Caleret and Roman.
The Roman.

And my brother also was born there. Then I had a sister, one of my sisters, she was born on Rayshelheim Street. And my other sister, the one that's living here on O'Reilly Street. Well, she was born on Rayshelheim Street. And Justin was born in Bay St. Louis.
Do you know if your father and uncle ever went back to Mexico to visit any relatives? Did you ever hear them say if they were going back to visit anyone? Well, I want to be frank with you.

You see, my father when he was living, he came down here. And the reason why we went to Bay St. Louis, I'm going to tell you. People here had a nice way of living. And like I told you, my father used to play with different bands. They were one. They were white and Negro. They made no difference in the relation. They were in the color as long as you were able to do something. That was the time in them days. Well, after this became the coming, my father then decided that he seemed to change. How did people begin to segregate?
Yeah, the prejudice and segregation came in after his lifetime.

So he told my mother, this is no place for us to raise our children. We got to get out of here. Well, he went to Bay St. Louis. Well, in Bay St. Louis everything was pretty cheap. You had house rent was cheaper. They had work. Then he had his music. He had his people just to send him orchestration to write from all parts of the city and different bands. He made money at it. He told my mother that he was going to write to the Mexican council, which he did. He had written to him and he told him that he wanted to come back to Mexico. Well, the council sent him a letter back. But he was, my father had taken sick. We moved from Bay St. Louis back here. Then the letter came in from Mexico. Told him to bring in all his, get all his papers set up to get him, bring him back. Come on back to Mexico and transportation and be paid. Then he, had he lived we wouldn't have been here. We wouldn't have been over there. We just went back in Mexico. Back to Mexico. Well, that's the...

When did your father die before I forget? I forgot to ask. About what year? If you don't remember exactly, you know, was it the time of the First World War or before? Must have been before that then. Alice. Oh, Alice. Yeah? Come here a minute please. Sorry to bother everybody. No, that's alright. These things are very interesting to us to do something like that.
Tell me something. How old were you when Papa died? Year and a half.
Year and a half.
Right. Now, this is urgent. What old are you now?
Fifty-four. That's why, alright. Fifty-four.
Fifty-four, so. Yeah. Now you see, he must have been dead.
I'll be fifty-five on the twenty-first day of January.
See, he's been dead now for... Fifty-three years.
That's right. That's right. That's right. Now, 1907 along in there then your father died. That's right. That's right. That's a long time ago, man. That's right.
